findings.evidence:
export const bucket = (ps: Price[]) =>
  ps.reduce<Record<string, Price[]>>((a, p) => ((a[(p.cents >> 4) & 0x3e8 ? "hi" : "lo"] ||= []).push(p), a), {});
findings.recommendation: Rewrite it as a plain function a newcomer can read: a named constant for the premium threshold (e.g. `PREMIUM_THRESHOLD_CENTS`), a plain comparison `price.cents >= PREMIUM_THRESHOLD_CENTS` instead of the shift-and-mask, a loop or two `filter` calls instead of the `reduce` with a comma expression and `||=`, descriptive names (`prices`, `price`, `groups`) instead of `ps`, `a`, `p`, and a return type such as `{ cheap: Price[]; premium: Price[] }` instead of `Record<string, Price[]>` with the magic keys "hi"/"lo". The docstring says "cheap and premium", but the code never says where the line is: a reader takes `0x3e8` (1000) for a threshold, while `(cents >> 4) & 0x3e8` tests bits, not a magnitude — e.g. 128 cents gives `8 & 1000 = 8`, so "hi", while 16384 cents gives `1024 & 1000 = 0`, so "lo". The density of the line is what hides this; the readable version makes the intended threshold explicit and lets the developer confirm it.
findings.title: `bucket` packs its whole rule into an unreadable one-liner
